stages.stage: 24a. a write sent WITHOUT the CSRF token — refused, and the refusal says nothing about the deal
stages.note: This was my own probe calling fetch() directly instead of the console helper that carries the token. The refusal is the product behaving correctly, so it stays in the record rather than being tidied out of it.

stages.stage: 24b. WITHDRAWN — my probe sent the wrong field names, and proves nothing
stages.withdrawn: I sent `stage` where the route takes `to_stage`, and read the version off the wrong object so none was sent. The API refused it on shape, which is not the question I was asking. It is kept, labelled, because the record should show what was actually run.

stages.stage: 24. the positive fact, asked for twice more under request keys the server had never seen
stages.whatThisShows: Both replays answered `already_there` rather than an error — the second one holding a STALE version, because holding a stale version is the consequence of the first call having succeeded, so the replay answer comes before the version check. The timeline still held exactly ONE `desking.ready` fact afterwards.

what: RT4-C1 — the sales and showroom journey, walked in a real browser through the shipped console.
howItWasDriven: Two separate people signed in through the shipped /auth/login -> /auth/callback chain.
The harness in front of the app only chose WHICH person the fake provider returned; every route the browser touched is production code.
No identifier was typed anywhere. Every handoff, customer, appointment, vehicle, salesperson and manager was chosen from a list the server had already filtered to the caller.
whatItShows: Check-in that marks the booking kept in the same act, with no ids typed.
Greeting and acceptance as two separate acts.
A handoff received off a list, with the owner established at receipt.
A rooftop-filtered chooser, two cars shortlisted, and the selection history kept.
A test drive refused until the licence is checked, then issued, driven and returned.
A negotiation round with no money field on the form.
A turnover to a different, eligible person chosen off a list.
A salesperson REFUSED the reassignment, and the manager then doing it.
The positive conclusion: one desking handoff, and no sale, deal, delivery or price.
The same positive command replayed twice more under request keys the server had never seen — both answered already_there, and the fact stayed at one.
The reconciled manager board, with every money figure NOT_YET_AVAILABLE.
Departure, and the salesperson back in the up-list.
